criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Identifies marketing brochure guarantee language as creating express warranties
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively discusses the brochure's guarantee language as creating express warranties under UCC § 2-313. In Part V (Issue 2), the memo explicitly identifies the brochure's '99.97% contaminant removal' guarantee language, notes it is labeled 'guaranteed' and paired with 'or we'll make it right — guaranteed,' and analyzes how these specific, measurable statements constitute express warranties under § 2-313. The memo also references this language in the Bottom Line section, Part III.B (the marketing statements table), and Part IV, consistently treating the brochure guarantee language as creating express warranty obligations that cannot be disclaimed under § 2-316(1).

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Identifies sales deck 'Our Promise to You' as creating express warranties
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly identifies the sales deck as creating express warranties under UCC § 2-313. In Part V.C.4, the document-by-document assessment table rates the sales deck as 'Critical' and specifically references 'Slide 7 "Our Promise to You": "make customers whole"' along with slides 17/13 'guaranteed' as creating express warranty issues. The memo also notes in Part V.C.2 that the specific, measurable performance figures in the deck cannot be dismissed as puffery, and in Part V.C.5 discusses the cumulative effect of all materials including the deck. The 'Our Promise to You' slide language is directly cited as warranty-creating content under § 2-313.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Identifies verbal sales representative instructions as warranty-creating conduct
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively analyzes the January 8 sales memo and its instructions to sales representatives as a critical source of express warranty creation. In Part V.C.2, the memo explicitly states that the sales memo 'Mandates guaranteed language in every customer interaction; bans hedging; instructs reps to tailor performance commitments (§ 2-315 fitness warranty); scripts make customers whole as the answer to consequential-damages questions.' The memo rates the sales memo as 'Critical' risk and notes that 'Oral statements create express warranties just as written ones do.' It also notes that the sales memo tells reps that performance figures are 'the numbers we commit to' and that 'do not hedge' instruction converts marketing claims into binding commitments. The memo further identifies that the 'make customers whole' scripting creates 'waiver/estoppel and misrepresentation exposure.' This clearly satisfies the criterion of identifying verbal/oral sales representative commitments as a source of express warranty risk.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Explains that existing disclaimer cannot override express warranties under UCC § 2-316(1)
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly addresses UCC § 2-316(1) in multiple places. In the Bottom Line section, it states: 'Under UCC § 2-316(1), fine print cannot cancel an express warranty that is inconsistent with it.' In Part V.C.6, it provides a detailed explanation: 'Where words creating an express warranty and words negating it cannot reasonably be read together, "negation or limitation is inoperative." A guarantee of 99.97% removal cannot reasonably coexist with "Seller makes no warranty regarding the results that may be obtained from the use of the Products" (SLW § 5). The express warranty prevails.' The memo clearly explains that the disclaimer cannot override the express warranties created by marketing materials and sales conduct under § 2-316(1).

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Recommends reconciling marketing language with warranty framework
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively addresses the conflict between marketing language and the warranty framework, and provides specific recommendations to reconcile them. In Part X (Recommendations), the memo recommends: (1) withdrawing the January 8 sales memo and stopping 'guaranteed/make customers whole/do not hedge' language; (2) removing unsubstantiated regulatory claims (WFI, '21 CFR Part 11 compliant,' 'validated for GMP,' 'ensures' FDA/EPA compliance, 'eliminates' recall risk); (3) revising the brochure and deck to keep figures but add a clear prominent line directing customers to the written Performance Warranty; (4) replacing 'make customers whole' and 'Period.' language; (5) creating a defined 'AquaPure Max 9000 Performance Warranty' with specific metrics, conditions, and remedies that Sales can brand as the 'Total Performance Guarantee'; (6) replacing 'your water will meet or exceed all EPA and state standards' with a statement of specific contaminant limits under defined conditions; and (7) providing specific acceptable vs. not acceptable language for sales reps. The memo also provides a core restructuring approach (Part IX.A) that explicitly converts the open-ended marketing promise into a defined contractual commitment. These are specific, actionable recommendations that directly reconcile the marketing language with the warranty framework.

It cites UCC § 1-201(b)(10) and references Cate v. Dover Corp. regarding the same typeface and size issue. criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Cites UCC § 1-201(b)(10) conspicuousness standard
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly cites UCC § 1-201(b)(10) in Part IV.C.2 when discussing conspicuousness: 'Conspicuousness (§ 1-201(b)(10)). A term is conspicuous if "a reasonable person against which it is to operate ought to have noticed it."' It also lists § 1-201(b)(10) in Appendix A as a key UCC provision referenced. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Recommends specific formatting improvements for conspicuousness
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly recommends specific formatting changes in Part IV.C.2: 'BSK's 2021 formatting recommendations should be implemented now: bold, larger type, a bordered or shaded box, a stand-alone "IMPORTANT --- DISCLAIMER OF WARRANTIES" heading, and buyer initials.' It also recommends the same treatment for §§ 4 and 6. In Part X.C.2 (Revised SLW), it again specifies 'enhanced conspicuousness (bold, larger type, boxed, stand-alone heading, initials) for §§ 4--6.' These are specific, concrete formatting recommendations beyond merely identifying the issue.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Identifies post-sale delivery of warranty terms as a critical deficiency
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively discusses the post-sale delivery of warranty terms as a critical deficiency. In Part IV.C.3 ('Assent and timing: the threshold defect'), the memo explicitly identifies that the SLW arrives 'weeks or months later, in the crate' and that this means it probably never becomes part of the contract. It cites UCC §§ 2-207 and 2-209, discusses the rolling contract cases and why they don't apply to large industrial units, and notes that BSK called this the 'highest-priority' issue in 2021. The memo also notes the January 8 sales memo instructs reps to withhold the warranty, converting an oversight into documented intent. This is flagged as the 'threshold defect' and listed as the first and most important reason the SLW is unlikely to be enforced. The memo also references this issue repeatedly throughout (Part I bottom line item 2, Part III.B, Part V.C.3, Part X recommendations). The criterion is clearly satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: References shrinkwrap/box-top enforceability case law or doctrine
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly references the shrinkwrap/box-top enforceability doctrine in Part IV.C.3, citing ProCD, Inc. v. Zeidenberg (86 F.3d 1447, 7th Cir. 1996) and Hill v. Gateway 2000, Inc. (105 F.3d 1147, 7th Cir. 1997) as the 'rolling contract' cases that uphold terms-in-the-box, while also noting their limitations (consumer mass-market goods that can be returned) and contrasting them with Step-Saver Data Systems, Inc. v. Wyse Technology (939 F.2d 91, 3d Cir. 1991), which treated post-formation box-top terms as § 2-207 proposals. The memo discusses the doctrinal split and explains why the rolling contract cases are hard to extend to the Max 9000 situation.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Notes that 2021 Birchwood memo recommended pre-sale disclosure and CIT failed to implement
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly references the 2021 Birchwood, Sato & Klein memorandum and notes that pre-sale disclosure was its 'highest-priority' recommendation. In Part IV.C.3, the memo states: 'BSK reached the same conclusion in 2021 and called it the "highest-priority" issue. It has not been fixed, and the January 8 sales memo now instructs reps to *withhold* the warranty.' This directly satisfies the criterion by noting both the prior outside counsel recommendation on pre-sale disclosure and CIT's failure to implement it.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Recommends integrating warranty terms into pre-sale documentation
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly and repeatedly recommends integrating warranty terms into pre-sale documentation. In Part IV.C.3, it identifies the post-sale delivery of the SLW as the 'threshold defect' and explains that terms presented after contract formation likely never become part of the contract. In Part X.B (Immediate Actions), item 8 recommends revising the Quotation Template to attach the SLW, Performance Warranty, and software terms as exhibits and replacing the 'included with product delivery' language. In Part X.C, it recommends building a 'Max 9000 Master Purchase Agreement (or Terms of Sale) incorporating the SLW (revised), the Performance Warranty, and the AquaMonitor terms' that 'is signed by the buyer before the deposit, with a separately initialed disclaimer and limitation block,' explicitly noting this 'single step fixes the assent defect.' The memo also notes this pre-sale signature supplies 'actual knowledge' under Texas law (Cate v. Dover Corp.). These recommendations clearly satisfy the criterion of recommending integration of warranty terms into pre-sale documents.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Analyzes implied warranty of fitness for particular purpose under UCC § 2-315
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively analyzes UCC § 2-315 fitness for particular purpose warranty risk in connection with CIT's customer-specific sales conduct. In Part IV.C.3, it explicitly states that the fitness warranty is 'especially potent here, because the sales memo tells reps to "tailor performance commitments" to each customer's water challenges and regulatory needs. That is the § 2-315 fact pattern: the seller has reason to know the particular purpose, and the buyer relies on the seller's skill.' In Part V.C (the sales memo analysis), it notes the memo 'instructs reps to tailor performance commitments (§ 2-315 fitness warranty).' In the California section, it identifies the agricultural representations and the instruction to describe the product as 'specifically designed' for seasonal demand fluctuations as 'a § 2-315 fitness-for-purpose invitation.' The memo connects the § 2-315 analysis directly to the specific customer applications (municipal water treatment for Triton, food processing for Great Lakes, agricultural for Harmon Valley, pharmaceutical for Massachusetts buyers) and to the sales practice of customizing performance commitments per customer. This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Explains that disclaimer effectiveness is undermined by sales conduct inviting reliance
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly addresses the tension between the disclaimer and CIT's sales conduct in multiple places. In Part IV.C.3, it notes that the fitness warranty (§ 2-315) is 'especially potent here, because the sales memo tells reps to "tailor performance commitments" to each customer's water challenges and regulatory needs. That is the § 2-315 fact pattern: the seller has reason to know the particular purpose, and the buyer relies on the seller's skill.' The memo also notes in Part V.C.1 that the sales memo instructs reps to 'tailor performance commitments' which is a § 2-315 fitness warranty invitation, and in Part VI.B (California) it again flags the same instruction as a 'fitness-for-purpose invitation.' The memo further explains that the disclaimer cannot be effective because it arrives post-sale and is inconsistent with the express warranties created by the marketing materials. The memo directly connects the sales conduct (scripted guarantees, tailored performance commitments, 'make customers whole' language) to the undermining of the disclaimer's effectiveness, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively addresses Texas-specific warranty and procurement risks for the Triton Municipal Water Authority deal. This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Flags California Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act risk for Harmon Valley deal
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo does mention the Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act in the California section (Part VI.B), but it concludes that it is 'unlikely to reach this sale directly' and that an industrial purification unit bought by a co-op for irrigation and processing 'is not a consumer good.' The memo explicitly dismisses Song-Beverly applicability rather than flagging it as a risk. The criterion requires the memo to identify that the Harmon Valley deal raises 'potential applicability' of Song-Beverly, noting that agricultural cooperatives purchasing goods for use by members 'could arguably fall within the Act's scope as consumer goods purchasers,' and that Song-Beverly imposes more restrictive disclaimer limitations than standard UCC Article 2. The memo does the opposite—it affirmatively concludes Song-Beverly does not apply and does not flag it as a risk or note that the co-op structure could arguably bring it within scope. Therefore, the criterion is not satisfied.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Analyzes failure of essential purpose doctrine under UCC § 2-719(2)
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively analyzes UCC § 2-719(2) failure of essential purpose doctrine in Part VIII. It explains the legal framework (§ 2-719(1) and (2)), discusses the split between independent and dependent approaches to consequential damages exclusions when the remedy fails, and applies this to CIT's situation with specific facts: lengthening resolution times (28→35→47 days), full-unit replacements taking 78-85 days, the remedy mismatch between repair/replace and performance guarantees, CIT's own 'make customers whole' language, the recurring pressure-vessel defect, and the $680,000 already paid in FY2024 settlements on failure-of-essential-purpose arguments. The memo clearly states that if the repair remedy fails, buyers may pursue full UCC remedies including consequential damages, and analyzes why the consequential damages exclusion may not survive.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Addresses whether consequential damages exclusion is independent of or dependent on exclusive remedy
criteria_results.reasoning: Section VIII.A explicitly discusses the case law split between the 'independent' approach (consequential damages exclusion survives even when the exclusive remedy fails of its essential purpose) and the 'dependent' approach (exclusion falls with the failed remedy), citing Chatlos Systems, Kearney & Trecker, and RRX Industries. It also notes a case-by-case unconscionability approach. Section VIII.B then applies this framework to the Max 9000, noting that SLW § 6 expressly states the limitations apply 'regardless of whether any remedy fails of its essential purpose' and are 'independent of' the exclusive remedy, while also explaining why the risk remains high despite this drafting.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Identifies software component warranty gap for AquaMonitor v3.2
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively addresses the AquaMonitor v3.2 software warranty gap in Issue 4 (Part VII). It explicitly states that SLW § 3.1 warrants freedom from 'defects in materials and workmanship' and that 'Product' is defined by listing hardware components. It then directly notes: 'Software is not "material," and coding errors are not naturally "workmanship."' The memo also discusses the UCC Article 2 applicability question, noting courts apply a 'predominant purpose' test and that embedded software is generally treated as goods, but that cloud subscription components are services governed by common-law principles. The memo identifies this as potentially CIT's 'largest unaddressed exposure' and details both the coverage gap (what CIT warrants) and the protection gap (whether the disclaimer reaches the software). This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Recommends addressing software in warranty framework
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo dedicates an entire section (Issue 3/Part VII) to the AquaMonitor software gap and provides detailed recommendations in Part VII.C. It explicitly recommends creating 'separate software terms': an AquaMonitor Software License and Subscription Agreement. The memo lists nine specific items to include: limited software warranty, statement that AquaMonitor is a decision-support tool not replacing customer regulatory obligations, sensor calibration allocation, data accuracy disclaimers and uptime/SLA commitments, OTA update terms, cybersecurity responsibilities and incident notification, data ownership, Part 11 language recast, and a software-specific liability cap. It also recommends amending the SLW definition of 'Product' to expressly extend hardware disclaimer and cap to embedded software, firmware, and data. This clearly satisfies the criterion of recommending that CIT address the software component in its warranty framework.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: Identifies sole-source filter cartridge warranty conditioning issue
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo does not mention CIT being the sole-source supplier of replacement filter cartridges at $8,500 each required every 6 months, nor does it discuss any legal risks related to conditioning warranty coverage on the use of CIT's own replacement cartridges, including tying concerns under antitrust law or Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act implications. The only reference to 'genuine cartridges' appears briefly in Part X.A as a condition of the Performance Warranty, but there is no discussion of sole-source supply, pricing, or the legal risks of such conditioning.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Identifies disconnect between quotation letter performance specs and warranty scope
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly identifies the disconnect between the quotation letter's performance specifications and the warranty's narrow 'materials and workmanship' scope. In Part IV.C.5, the memo states: 'Coverage limited to "materials and workmanship" (§ 3.1). This excludes design defects and performance shortfalls. It does not match the product CIT is actually selling. Design-based performance shortfalls, such as a membrane that cannot reach 99.97% on certain feed water, would fall *outside* the SLW entirely and be governed only by the marketing warranties.' The memo also notes in Part V.B.4 that the quotation letter is 'The most dangerous in legal structure' and discusses how the 99.97% and 98.5% figures in the quotation letter constitute express warranties under § 2-313. The memo further cross-references this issue in Part X.C.2, recommending that § 3.1 be 'cross-referenced to the Performance Warranty, so there is no conflict between "materials and workmanship only" and the guarantee.' This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011a: References escalating warranty claims trend data
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo includes a detailed claims trend table in Section III.C showing FY2022: 47 claims/$1.34M, FY2023: 62 claims/$1.87M, FY2024: 71 claims/$2.21M, which exactly matches the criterion's required figures.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011b: Connects warranty claims trend data to legal analysis
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively connects the warranty claims trend data to legal analysis. In Part VIII.B, it explicitly links the rising resolution times (28→35→47 days, full replacements at 78-85 days) to the § 2-719(2) 'failure of essential purpose' doctrine, noting that 'failure to repair within a reasonable time is the most commonly successful § 2-719(2) argument.' It connects the $680,000 in FY2024 consequential-damages settlements to the argument that the remedy is already failing. It notes the Max 9000's higher price point means a single replacement costs $475,000-$525,000 before consequential damages, amplifying risk. The memo also connects the recurring pressure-vessel defect pattern (six failures) to the legal standard that courts treat such patterns as evidence the seller cannot cure. The quantified risk projections in Part VIII.D explicitly tie the claims trend to projected Max 9000 exposure. The memo directly states the claims history shows courts 'already are' resolving the contradiction against CIT. This is a thorough connection between claims data and legal conclusions about remedy failure and amplified risk from the new product launch.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011c: References FY2024 consequential damage claims data
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly references the FY2024 consequential damage claims data. In Section III.C, it notes '$680,000' in consequential-damages settlements for FY2024. It also specifically identifies WC-2024-022 (Meridian Pharmaceutical, $145,000 settlement), WC-2024-039 (Cascade Bottling Works, $535,000 settlement), and WC-2024-063 (Redmond Beverage Distributors, $1.2M claimed, in litigation). The two settled claims together total $680,000, and the Redmond pending claim for $1.2M is also referenced. All three FY2024 consequential damage claims are present in the memo.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_011d: Uses consequential damage claims to support analysis of exclusion adequacy
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo extensively connects the FY2024 consequential damage claims and the Redmond litigation to the legal analysis of the consequential damages exclusion and remedy provisions. In Part VIII (Issue 5), the memo explicitly uses the $680,000 in FY2024 consequential-damages settlements as evidence that the repair-or-replace remedy is already failing in practice, noting that 'CIT paid $680,000 in FY2024 to settle consequential-damages claims that argued the remedy had failed of its essential purpose.' The Redmond litigation is analyzed in detail, including the buyer's theory that the sales-presentation specification is an express warranty, the remedy failed of its essential purpose, and the consequential-damages exclusion falls with it. The memo also uses these facts to assess the durability of the § 2-719 exclusion, noting that the settlements 'signal that CIT does not trust its own remedy clause' and will be used by plaintiffs' counsel. The analysis directly ties the claims history to the legal framework (§ 2-719(2) failure of essential purpose, the independent vs. dependent split), and uses them to rate the risk as high. This is a clear, substantive connection between the factual claims record and the legal analysis of the exclusion's adequacy.
